name: Middle cerebral artery
summary: The larger terminal branch of the internal carotid and the artery most often occluded in stroke. The M1 segment runs laterally beneath the anterior perforated substance, giving the lateral lenticulostriate perforators to the basal ganglia and internal capsule, then splits in the Sylvian fissure into superior and inferior divisions whose cortical branches cover almost the entire lateral convexity: motor and sensory cortex for face and arm, Broca's and Wernicke's areas, the frontal eye field, the insula and the parietal association cortex.

anatomy.location: From the carotid terminus the horizontal M1 segment passes laterally in the Sylvian cistern below the anterior perforated substance to the limen insulae, where it divides (M2 segments run over the insula, M3 segments turn around the opercula, M4 branches spread across the convexity).

subdivisions.name: M1 (sphenoidal)
subdivisions.note: lateral lenticulostriate perforators; anterior temporal branch

subdivisions.name: Superior division
subdivisions.note: orbitofrontal, prefrontal, precentral, central and anterior parietal branches: frontal and anterior parietal convexity

subdivisions.name: Inferior division
subdivisions.note: posterior parietal, angular and temporal branches: posterior parietal and lateral temporal cortex

relations.superior: anterior perforated substance, through which the lenticulostriate arteries enter
relations.lateral: temporal lobe below and frontal operculum above in the Sylvian fissure

function: Supplies the lateral surface of the hemisphere except the superior strip taken by the ACA and the occipital pole and inferior temporal surface taken by the PCA. This includes the face, hand and arm areas of the motor and sensory cortices, the frontal eye field, Broca's area, Wernicke's area, the auditory cortex, the insula and, through the lenticulostriates, the putamen, globus pallidus, caudate body and the anterior and superior parts of the internal capsule.

bestView.label: M1 segment in the Sylvian cistern and the bifurcation at the limen insulae
convexity territory: frontal and parietal opercula

imaging.normalAppearance: M1 is a prominent flow void lateral to the carotid terminus on axial T2; branches in the Sylvian fissure appear as dots within CSF. On non-contrast CT the M1 segment may look denser than other vessels when thrombosed (hyperdense MCA sign).

pathology.finding: Early signs: hyperdense M1, loss of the insular ribbon, obscuration of the lentiform nucleus and sulcal effacement; later a wedge of hypodensity over the lateral convexity with mass effect peaking at 3–5 days.
pathology.timing: Early signs within 1–3 h; hypodensity by 6–12 h; maximal swelling day 3–5

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the insula, opercular cortex and lateral convexity, with a lentiform and capsular component when M1 is occluded proximal to the lenticulostriates; FLAIR vascular hyperintensities mark slow collateral flow.
pathology.timing: DWI positive within minutes; FLAIR after ~6 h (the DWI–FLAIR mismatch estimates onset)

pathology.finding: Saccular aneurysm at the M1 bifurcation in the Sylvian fissure; rupture gives Sylvian and temporal lobe hematoma.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Non-contrast CT plus CTA in the acute phase to identify a large-vessel occlusion amenable to thrombectomy; DWI/FLAIR for infarct extent and timing

lesionEffects.mechanism: Precentral gyrus face and hand areas on the convexity
Postcentral gyrus and parietal association cortex
Frontal eye field: the intact hemisphere drives the eyes away from itself
Broca's and Wernicke's areas both within the territory
Optic radiation in the deep parietal and temporal white matter

examination: Compare arm drift with leg drift: MCA infarcts weaken the arm more than the leg
Assess speech fluency, comprehension and repetition
Look for gaze deviation and test for visual and tactile extinction
pearls: Face and arm weakness plus aphasia or neglect is the MCA; leg-predominant weakness is the ACA
A dense hemiplegia involving the leg too with an MCA occlusion means the lenticulostriates (internal capsule) are involved, i.e. an M1 occlusion
Malignant MCA infarction in the young can require decompressive craniectomy within 48 hours

pitfalls: Isolated hand weakness can be a small cortical MCA branch infarct and is easily mistaken for a peripheral nerve lesion
Wernicke aphasia without weakness may be labeled confusion or psychosis
